Demons, also called The Possessed, is Dostoevsky's caustic political novel from 1872. It depicts a revolutionary cell infiltrating a provincial Russian town, exposing the spiritual emptiness and destructive amorality of radical ideologies. The brilliant manipulator Pyotr Verkhovensky orchestrates murder and conspiracy to unmask the pretensions of socialist revolution, while the passive intellectual Nikolai Stavrogin becomes an unwitting idol for their nihilist movement. The title alludes to the biblical story of demons entering swine. Dostoevsky frames radical politics as spiritual possession, a form of demonic madness rather than rational reform. Pyotr Verkhovensky is a Machiavellian schemer who fabricates a secret society and orchestrates murders to advance his vision of destruction and remake Russian society through terror. Nikolai Stavrogin is brilliant and amoral. He becomes the great man around whom the radicals gather, yet his confession and suicide expose the void at the heart of the conspiracy. The novel features a famous revolutionary manifesto and depicts how cynical manipulation can exploit genuine social discontent for destructive ends. Dostoevsky drew inspiration from the Nechayev conspiracy of eighteen sixty-nine, a real revolutionary cell and murder that scandalized Russia. Published serially in The Russian Messenger, the novel was banned in Russia until nineteen-oh-six. Its political pessimism made it controversial across the ideological spectrum. Today it reads as a prophetic warning written decades before the Russian Revolution of nineteen seventeen. Through this fierce satire, Dostoevsky exposes the spiritual disease he diagnoses in European radical thought.
